top_choice_rationale: Tawada (P003) remains my first choice, though the margin over Cărtărescu is narrow. Writing across Japanese and German makes estrangement between languages a formal method rather than a theme. On public knowledge, The Emissary and Memoirs of a Polar Bear pair a light, precise, uncanny voice with real intellectual weight on language, migration and fragility. The same poetics continues across fiction, poetry, essays and drama for over three decades. I take that continuity as evidence of sustained quality, and I weigh it above architectural scale. The citation should name both languages, rest on the fiction and the formal method, and state the language of each work discussed. Cărtărescu (P001) is second because his cumulative prose project is the firmer ground if the bilingual method proves too thinly evidenced for a whole-oeuvre citation. Carson (P002) is third. I find her case serious and withdraw my round-1 doubt about her reach, but I cannot judge her design-dependent books from the text. No award (P000) is last because the shortlist contains candidates I can support on the stated criteria. Uncertainties: I cannot measure how much of Tawada's wordplay survives translation, and German-language texts, poetry and drama are least visible. I cannot say whether her later novels develop or restate the early invention. I have not read or independently verified any text. This judgment rests on public knowledge only.
recusal_note: none apparent from profile. It records no personal or institutional tie to Tawada, Cărtărescu, Carson or any other shortlisted writer. Her international translator engagements and her documented 2021 statement about women's literary work are context only, not evidence of a preference. Gender, nationality and language do not by themselves establish literary merit.
